Retracting the claim that the env script fails to export credentials: bin/provider-env/_fireworks_common.sh:80 exports ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (bearer) and :83 deliberately unsets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to prevent a stale x-api-key from shadowing it. The token is also valid — a direct probe of $ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/v1/messages with that bearer returns HTTP 200 with model=accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3.

## Root cause: the executing process tree is not a descendant of the lock holder

Reproduced this on Claude Code with a **backgrounded session**, and the "live lock-holder pid was a *different* pid" observation in the report turns out to be the whole story rather than a side detail.

`bin/fm-claude-stop-autoarm.sh` gates on `fm_session_lock_owned_by_self` (`bin/fm-session-lock-lib.sh`). That predicate reads `state/.lock` and walks `fm_harness_ancestry_pids` from the *calling* process looking for a match. When Claude runs work as a background job, there is no ancestral link to walk:

```
executing tree:   <shell> -> 30591 claude bg-spare -> 30579 claude bg-pty-host -> init(1)
                  started 15:16:48, pgid 30579, reparented to init

state/.lock:      27567 claude
                  started 15:07:53, pgid 27567, under the terminal multiplexer -> zsh -> login
```

Two unrelated trees, different process groups, nine minutes apart. The lock was acquired by the interactive `claude` at session start; the work then executes in a detached `bg-pty-host` / `bg-spare` tree. The ancestry walk from the executing side can never reach `27567`, so the predicate returns false.

Control then falls into the stale-owner branch:

```sh
if ! fm_session_lock_owned_by_self "$STATE"; then
  LOCK_PID=$(cat "$STATE/.lock" ...)
  ...
  fm_harness_pid_alive "$LOCK_PID" && exit 0   # <- always taken
  RECOVER_SESSION_LOCK=1
fi
```

`27567` is genuinely alive, so this is `exit 0` every single firing. That matches every symptom in the report: the epoch never advances, no failure-notice or failure-alarm file is ever written, manual invocation exits 0 with no output, and only a manual `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` ever starts a watcher. `fm_supervision_needed` returned true throughout, so the need gate was not involved.

## Why it is hard to see

This branch is a **silent** `exit 0`. It writes no marker, no diagnostic and no failure epoch, so the only thing that surfaces it is the turn-end guard refusing to end the turn. If the guard's bounded attended fail-open ever lets a stop through, supervision is off and nothing says so. Recording an observable "inert because not lock owner" reason would have made this diagnosable immediately.

## Constraint on any fix

The stale-owner branch exists so a genuinely new session can take over a dead session's lock. A fix that simply relaxes the identity check risks two live sessions both claiming supervision. The identity signal needs to recognise a detached background tree as the same session while still distinguishing a *different* session - process group or session identity rather than pid ancestry, or having the lock record something the background tree can independently prove.

## Environment

Claude Code primary, backgrounded session, macOS. Session lock held and valid the whole time (`bin/fm-lock.sh status` reported a live harness pid); both `Stop` hooks correctly registered.

The head of this PR moved from `704dd7ed` to `6b82660c`. Recording why.

The original head was raised outside this repository's required submission path, so the branch was resubmitted through it. That resubmission rebased onto current `main`, which rewrote the existing commit hashes without changing their content.

Two things were then added on top of the original work.

**Test portability fix.** The new stale-index cases in `tests/fm-teardown.test.sh` advanced the branch from a second worktree using `git checkout -B`, which git refuses once another worktree already holds that branch. Git 2.41.0 allows the same sequence, so the suite passed on the machine it was written on while CI on ubuntu-24.04 aborted the whole file with exit 128 before any assertion ran:

```
fatal: 'fm/task-x1' is already used by worktree at '.../stale-index-allow/wt'
```

The second copy now stays detached and the branch ref moves with `git update-ref`, which no git version guards. Same observable precondition, verified green under both git 2.41.0 and git 2.50.1.

**Review and documentation corrections**, in `bin/fm-teardown.sh`, `bin/fm-spawn.sh`, `docs/configuration.md` and `docs/verification/supervision.md`. Of note: the claim that hooks in a copy's `.claude/settings.local.json` still fire alongside an operator supplied `--settings` file was previously untested, and is now verified empirically on Claude Code 2.1.223 with the evidence recorded in `docs/verification/supervision.md`.

The root cause comments in `bin/fm-teardown.sh` also no longer name `git checkout -B <branch> origin/<branch>` in a second worktree as the mechanism, since git refuses that. They now key on the resulting index shape instead.

A later lint fix moved the head once more after this note was first written; `6b82660c` is the final head.

A second operator-side observation clarifies defect A and its acceptance criteria.

My normal primary Firstmate session runs in Ghostty and intentionally is **not** inside tmux. This has been the working operator surface for weeks; moving the primary session into tmux is not an acceptable mitigation. In that environment, `$TMUX_PANE` being absent is expected and does not mean that no operator session exists.

That makes the current fallback more than a bad guess:

```text
TMUX_PANE absent
→ target discovery cannot name the actual Ghostty-hosted operator session
→ fallback resolves to firstmate:0
→ firstmate:0 belongs to a crew/login shell, not the active operator session
→ the strict composer guard correctly refuses to inject
→ escalation and its warning never reach the operator
```

The strict composer guard should remain. The missing capability is an operator-session identity that does not depend on tmux ancestry.

Suggested acceptance criteria for defect A:

1. **Ghostty/non-tmux positive case.** Start Firstmate from an ordinary Ghostty shell with `TMUX_PANE` unset. Arm away mode and deliver a synthetic escalation. The escalation reaches the exact initiating operator session; no tmux session or `firstmate:0` target is required.
2. **No constant-as-discovery.** If the operator session cannot be identified or is ambiguous, the pane channel reports an explicit unavailable/degraded verdict. It must not convert absence into `firstmate:0` and call that a discovered target.
3. **Identity is bound at session start.** Record a concrete runtime-independent operator-session handle when the primary session starts, then bind away-mode delivery to that handle. Re-check that it still names the same live session before injection.
4. **Wrong-target negative.** Create an unrelated `firstmate:0` login/crew shell alongside the real Ghostty session. The escalation must never be delivered to or classified through that shell.
5. **tmux remains supported.** A genuine `TMUX_PANE` target continues to work, but it is one provider of operator-session identity rather than a required operator workflow.
6. **Independent alarm path.** If the bound channel cannot deliver for the configured threshold, the alert leaves through a channel independent of the failed injection path and names the actual diagnosis: target source, target identity, composer classification, and elapsed failure period.

This is distinct from #1654's Herdr/composer-readability repair. That work may fix a correct target that cannot be read. It does not supply the missing operator identity when the valid primary surface is Ghostty outside tmux.

Environment scope: observed on macOS with Ghostty; no claim that every terminal exposes the same session primitive. The required property is runtime-independent operator identity or an explicit refusal, not a Ghostty-specific hard-coded path.

## Owed record: E2E reproduction evidence, and one deliberately accepted residual

Two items the captain asked to have on this PR. They are recorded here so they survive
body regeneration on re-validation; they will also be folded into the intent when this
branch is re-validated.

---

### 1. End-to-end reproduction, before and after

Run in a **throwaway isolated firstmate home** (its own `FM_HOME`, state, and registry -
never the main home or a live one), driving the real path end to end: a real armed source,
the real blocking cursor-anchored delta reader over the real remote entrypoint, the real
process-event runner, and the real wake queue. **Nothing about the ingest is stubbed.**

The reproduction acts exactly as firstmate acted in the incident: on the published wake it
runs only the **generic** runner acknowledgement, and nothing else. That is deliberate -
it means every observation that passes after the fix comes from code, not from a handler
remembering to do the right thing.

Two scenarios:

- **A** - the reply arrives while the request is still open.
- **B** - the reply arrives after the request already escalated (the incident's own shape).

#### Before (base commit `8387039`)

```text
== Scenario A: reply arrives while the request is still open
retired: remote-reply-ios (adapter classified the captured result terminal)
captured: .../home/state/procevent-inbox/remote-reply-ios.1.result
  (the wake was published as expected)
  FAIL  the relay is still armed after the wake was handled
  FAIL  the reply reached the local status mirror
  FAIL  the answered request resolved instead of escalating
  PASS  no false missed-report escalation was raised
  FAIL  the open-decisions fold is clear
== Scenario B: reply arrives after the request already escalated
  (the request escalated as a missed report, as the incident did)
retired: remote-reply-ios (adapter classified the captured result terminal)
captured: .../home/state/procevent-inbox/remote-reply-ios.2.result
  FAIL  the late reply reached the local status mirror
  FAIL  the late reply resolved the escalated request
  FAIL  the settled request stopped surfacing in the open-decisions fold

RESULT: FAILURE REPRODUCED (7 failed observations)
--- local status mirror ---
blocked: pending-reply-recovery-delivery-failed: task=ios pending-reply-id=7ee03e6a8aaf42e9 request=publish the release chain
blocked: pending-reply-missed: task=ios pending-reply-id=ff9c14d41d5043cc request=confirm the notarization
--- open decisions fold ---
default	blocked	pending-reply-missed: task=ios pending-reply-id=ff9c14d41d5043cc request=confirm the notarization
--- pending-reply records ---
7ee03e6a8aaf42e9 phase=escalated
ff9c14d41d5043cc phase=escalated
```

This confirmed the diagnosis before any fix was written: the delta is captured and
announced, the generic acknowledgement retires the wake, and the reply is never applied.
Both requests then escalate as missed reports for work the remote had actually completed,
and the fold keeps surfacing them.

It also exposed a consequence that was **not** part of the stated diagnosis: each capture
is terminal for its registration, and only the adapter's own handling re-arms the next one.
With that handling never running, the relay was left retired after every reply and only
came back because session start re-arms it.

#### After (this branch, at `c5f608b`)

```text
== Scenario A: reply arrives while the request is still open
retired: remote-reply-ios (adapter classified the captured result terminal)
autohandled: remote-reply-ios
captured: .../home/state/procevent-inbox/remote-reply-ios.1.result
  (the wake was published as expected)
  PASS  the relay is still armed after the wake was handled
  PASS  the reply reached the local status mirror
  PASS  the answered request resolved instead of escalating
  PASS  no false missed-report escalation was raised
  PASS  the open-decisions fold is clear
== Scenario B: reply arrives after the request already escalated
  (the request escalated as a missed report, as the incident did)
retired: remote-reply-ios (adapter classified the captured result terminal)
autohandled: remote-reply-ios
captured: .../home/state/procevent-inbox/remote-reply-ios.2.result
  PASS  the late reply reached the local status mirror
  PASS  the late reply resolved the escalated request
  PASS  the settled request stopped surfacing in the open-decisions fold

RESULT: relay behaved correctly end to end (0 failed observations)
```

Both halves of the fix were verified independently load-bearing by reverting one file at a
time and re-running the colocated regression:

- without the runner's adapter-owned application (`bin/fm-procevent.sh`):
  `not ok - the captured reply never reached the secondmate's local status mirror`
- without the escalation close (`bin/fm-pending-reply-lib.sh`):
  `not ok - the settled request still surfaces as an open decision`

Scope note for accuracy: the transcripts above are from that isolated-home reproduction at
`c5f608b`. The pipeline subsequently added further hardening on this branch - per-request
serialization of resolution against escalation, the guarded legacy close, the reserved key
namespace, and by-construction escalation matching. That later work is covered by the test
transcripts already in the PR body, not by the two transcripts above.

---

### 2. Deliberately accepted residual: the capture-to-apply crash sliver

Adapter-owned application is hooked into **capture only**, not into the watcher's
`reconcile`.

`reconcile` runs synchronously on the watcher's cycle, and putting a remote call there
could stall supervision for the whole fleet. That tradeoff was raised explicitly and the
captain accepted it.

The residual is therefore the narrow window in which the process crashes **after** a result
is durably captured but **before** it is applied. In that window the result is simply left
unacknowledged, which means it stays eligible for re-announcement and comes back to the
handler on a later drain or restart - the existing announce-until-handled backstop, plus
the corrected handling instruction in `.agents/skills/process-event-sources/SKILL.md`.

This is a deliberate, accepted residual rather than an oversight: the normal path is
guaranteed by code, and the crash path degrades to exactly the behavior that existed before
this change rather than to silent loss.

Pushed a second commit to this branch: 2d57d82 fixes the claim-lock hang that remained after the ancestry fix. On Git Bash/MSYS without symlink privilege, 'ln -s' silently copies the owner directory instead of linking, so the readlink ownership handshake never verifies and fm_lock_acquire_wait spins forever on its own copied claim (this also produced the nested .steal.steal debris). The fix creates claim locks as directory junctions (mklink /J, no privilege needed) on Windows, invoked under MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL so the MSYS runtime does not mangle the cmd.exe arguments. Non-Windows platforms keep plain 'ln -s'. Verified end-to-end on Windows 11 Home / Git Bash: session lock acquires in under a second, repeat acquires are stable, and a full session-start digest runs the mutating bootstrap path.

## Correction: one caveat on the evidence, and a scope check

The operator who hit this asked a fair question I had not ruled out — whether this is an artifact of updating firstmate **while a task was already running**. Checking `fc3684a..70aeba8`:

- `--resolve-key` is **new in this update** (6c206ed), so the worker whose decision I tried to close was spawned by the **previous** scaffold. That is why the mismatch surfaced only now.
- The matcher's expected placement is **not** new: `bin/fm-classify-lib.sh` documented `needs-decision [key=api-shape]:` at old line 155-156 before the update too.
- The ambiguous brief wording is present in **both** versions. The update reworded that sentence but kept the colon-first template and still does not say where the key goes:
  - before: ``append `resolved: {how it was decided or unblocked}` (keyed with `[key=<slug>]` if you opened it with one)``
  - after: ``append `resolved: {how it cleared}` yourself (keyed with `[key=<slug>]` if you opened it with one)``

So the mid-flight update explains the *timing*, not the defect: the scaffold/matcher mismatch predates the update and survives it, and the silent-until-now part is that nothing consumed the key before `--resolve-key` existed.

**What I did not verify, stated plainly:** all my observed status lines come from workers spawned by the pre-update scaffold. I have not yet confirmed that a worker spawned *after* the update also writes the colon-first form — the wording that would lead it there is still in the file, but that is inference, not a measurement. If a maintainer can reproduce with a freshly spawned worker, that closes the gap; if a post-update worker happens to emit the matched form, then this reduces to the wording being ambiguous rather than actively wrong, and the suggested fix (make 249/334/450 show the exact position) still applies.

Everything else in the original report is unchanged and was directly observed.
Keeping this rule as a local operational preference instead of a shared template change; closing without merging.

Confirming this from the other side of the same bug, with fresh evidence — the key-position mismatch also breaks **decision bookkeeping**, not just `--resolve-key`.

## Same cause, second symptom

A decision written the way the scaffold teaches:

```
needs-decision: [key=646-seq-gate] <summary>
```

registers under `default`, because `fm-classify-lib.sh` only reads `[key=]` **between the verb and the colon**. The crew then correctly writes the closing line in the matched form:

```
resolved [key=646-seq-gate]: <how it was decided>
```

…which closes a key that was never open. The original `default` registration stays open **permanently**. So `OPEN DECISIONS` keeps listing a decision that has already been answered, and no amount of correctly-keyed answering clears it. The only way out is hand-appending an unkeyed `resolved:` line.

## Frequency

**Five occurrences in one session on 2026-08-06**, across five independent crewmates on the same project — plus two more from my own supervisor-side writes. Every crew produced the wrong placement unprompted. That rate is the useful signal here: this is not crews being careless, it is the scaffold teaching the wrong shape.

## The prose fix is not sufficient — already tried upstream

Worth flagging before anyone fixes only the wording: current `origin/main`'s `bin/fm-brief.sh` **already mentions** `[key=<slug>]` (three occurrences), and crews still got it wrong every time.

The reason is that rule 6's **example** shows:

```
append `needs-decision: {summary of options}`
```

— colon immediately after the verb. A crew adding a key naturally appends it to that template, landing it after the colon. **The example is what needs fixing**, not the surrounding prose.

## On making the parser tolerant

Accepting both positions is the obvious alternative, and it is tempting. One caution from having looked at it: tolerance would **retroactively reinterpret existing status logs** — lines currently registered under `default` would suddenly resolve to a key, changing which decisions read as open in logs written under the old behaviour. If tolerance is the chosen fix, it probably wants to be forward-dated or paired with a migration, rather than applied to history.

Fixing the example is the smaller, safer change and would have prevented all seven of the cases above.

## The caveat in my own correction is now closed: reproduced on a worker spawned entirely post-update

In [my correction above](#) I flagged an honest gap: every status log I had examined belonged to a crewmate spawned by the **previous** scaffold, so I could not rule out that the mid-task update was itself the cause. That gap is now closed by a fresh observation on the same commit.

### What was different this time

A crewmate spawned **entirely under `70aeba8`** — brief scaffolded by the current `bin/fm-brief.sh`, launched well after the update landed, no pre-update state involved — parked a real ask-user decision and wrote:

```
needs-decision: [key=ucto-verze-doc-gate] no-mistakes document gate má 2 ask-user nálezy …
```

Answering it with the documented mechanism refused, byte-for-byte the same as before:

```
$ bin/fm-send.sh <task> --resolve-key ucto-verze-doc-gate '<decision>'
error: --resolve-key 'ucto-verze-doc-gate': no open decision or blocker with that key in
state/<task>.status (already closed, mistyped, or transferred). Re-check the OPEN DECISIONS
listing, then resend without that key or with the right one; nothing was sent.
```

`[key=ucto-verze-doc-gate]` was the only key in that log and the `needs-decision` line was the last line, with no `resolved` line anywhere — the same shape as the original report.

**Conclusion: the update explains the timing, not the defect.** `--resolve-key` is new in `6c206ed`, which is why nobody hit this before; the scaffold wording it disagrees with predates it. A fully post-update worker reproduces it, so there is nothing to attribute to updating mid-task.

### Which of the three sites is load-bearing for a ship brief

Worth pinning, since the suggested fix touches three lines: the wording a **ship** crewmate actually receives comes from **`bin/fm-brief.sh:334`**, rendered as line 91 of the generated brief:

> `Firstmate's reply normally writes that closing line at answer time; when a blocker or wait clears WITHOUT a firstmate reply, append `resolved: {how it cleared}` yourself (same `[key=<slug>]` if you opened it with one) …`

A worker following that line writes the key **after** the colon in both directions. `:249` and `:450` carry the same wording for the other brief variants, and `:246-247` shows the correct form — so a fix that changes only one of them will leave the others drifting exactly as they do today. That is the case for the regression test suggested in the original report: assert that a status line written **exactly as the brief instructs** is closable by `--resolve-key`.

### Downstream effect worth naming once

With answerer-closes unusable, the fallback is that the crewmate appends its own `resolved` line. That works, but it silently relocates the closing write from the answering side to the answered side — so the operator's answer and the record of it being answered are no longer produced by the same action. Nothing was lost here because the crew did append it, but it means a crew that forgets leaves a decision open forever with no error anywhere.

Another occurrence on 2026-08-08, in a secondmate home on the herdr backend with codex crews. Same slot handover and reset, but with two details that extend the report above.

**What happened.** A ship task had been working in pool slot 1 of its project, committed two documentation commits to its own branch, and then deliberately parked on an external dependency (`paused:`, waiting on a third-party support answer). Some time later a scout task was spawned for the same project. `treehouse get` handed out slot 1 again: both tasks' `state/<id>.meta` recorded the identical `worktree=` path, and the slot's reflog shows the handover reset in the expected place:

```
a153b262 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from fm/<ship-task> to refs/remotes/origin/<default-branch>
462de790 HEAD@{1}: commit: docs: <second commit>
da214875 HEAD@{2}: commit: docs: <first commit>
```

**Detail 1 - the spawn guard did not fire.** `bin/fm-spawn.sh` launched the scout into the occupied slot without refusing. The parked ship task's agent process had exited by the time of the spawn, so from a process-presence standpoint nothing owned the slot - which is exactly the signal this issue says is wrong, appearing a second time on the firstmate side rather than only in the pool. The durable evidence that the slot was owned was all present and none of it is process-shaped: a live `state/<id>.meta` naming that worktree, a task in `paused:` state in the durable status log, a backlog entry on hold, and a task branch with unlanded commits in that very checkout. A guard keyed on "another live task in this home records this worktree" cannot see an idle or exited-but-parked worker, and a deliberately parked task is precisely the case most likely to have no process.

**Detail 2 - the damage window is wider than two agents in one checkout.** Because the reset moved HEAD off the task branch, the parked task's own checkout no longer reflected its work, and ordinary teardown of *either* task would have targeted a slot the other still depended on. The commits survived only because the branch ref itself was untouched; that branch existed on no remote, so the branch ref was the single copy. Recovery here was to take a read-only `git bundle` of `<default-branch>..<task-branch>` outside the repo and freeze cleanup of both tasks, which is not something a caller should have to think of.

**What this supports.** It is further evidence for the suggested direction: explicit leases at ordinary task spawn. Process presence fails for the idle case in the pool, and the derived "live task" check in `fm-spawn` inherits the same blind spot, so both layers agree with each other and are wrong together. A lease taken at spawn and released at teardown would have made the slot unavailable while the task was parked, which is the state where this is most likely to bite.

## Same invariant at two further sites, not covered by the downstream patch

Reviewing the fix downstream surfaced two more places with the identical "reclaim removes only canonical names, then `rmdir`" shape.
Recording them here so the pattern is visible even though the patch deliberately does not cover them - each needs its own function and regression test, and both are pre-existing rather than regressions.

**1. Job claim directory - still permanent, nothing heals it.**
`bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh`, `worker_clear_dead_claim` and `worker_stop_recorded_execution`.
`worker_run_with_timeout` stages `$job/.claim/.group.XXXXXX` and `$job/.claim/.armed.XXXXXX` before renaming into place.
A SIGTERM inside that window is ordinary, since `fm_remote_job_ensure_worker` TERMs workers on every code-identity change.
The canonical-name removal skips the not-yet-published `group` and `armed` names, so the later `rmdir` of `$job/.claim` fails and keeps failing.
Unlike the ownership lock, no later path reclaims it.

**2. Reap leaks a job record permanently.**
`bin/fm-remote-job-lib.sh`, `fm_remote_job_reap`.
`worker_publish_result` stages `$job/.exit.XXXXXX` before renaming it to `exit`.
A SIGTERM in that window abandons the scratch while the job is still `running`; the next worker's `worker_recover_orphaned_job` republishes a result and the record legitimately reaches `done` with the dead worker's scratch still present.
`fm_remote_job_reap` then removes only canonical names before its `rmdir` of `$job/.claim` and `$job`, so reap returns non-zero permanently and the record leaks.

**One further site inside the ownership lock itself**, which the downstream patch does cover indirectly: `worker_supervisor_cleanup_dead_child` releases the same `worker.lock` without clearing scratch.
On its own that would let the original wedge reappear through the Linux supervisor path, so the downstream change adds the scratch clear there too.
Worth noting that even without it the reclaim fix degrades that path to roughly a 10 second `worker_lock_recent` stall rather than a permanent wedge.

If it is useful, the general shape is to give the worker one owned "remove my staged scratch from this directory" helper and call it from every site that stages through `mktemp` before `rmdir`, instead of teaching each reclaim site its own list.

I reproduced this on Pi + Herdr during a 16.0-hour away-mode interval. There were 94 operational messages that required no action: 72 paused-wait digests, 14 heartbeats, 2 stale rechecks, and 6 missing-supervision alarms. The 72 paused-wait messages contained 13 distinct payloads, so 59 were repeat deliveries of an unchanged payload after it had visibly arrived.

Those messages caused 120 model calls. Pi's session usage records show 7,592,777 processed tokens: 6,939,136 cache-read tokens, 647,320 uncached input tokens, and 6,321 output tokens, at $6.90 recorded cost. That is 5.86 needless interruptions, 473,218 processed tokens, and $0.43 per wall-clock hour. The interval includes time the laptop was powered off, so the hourly rate understates the rate while it was actually running.

67 of the final responses were exactly `Captain, shipshape.` Those alone accounted for 4,412,528 processed tokens and $3.14. Restarting away mode cleared the buffer temporarily, but the same behavior returned after the next paused-wait reminder.

I found this after opening #2043 for the same OMP adapter goal. I am consolidating that work here and will close #2043 once the missing behavior below is represented.

Verified evidence worth preserving:

- A real `fm-spawn.sh` OMP worker completed an external task and opened SuresoftTechnologies/verifai-issue-tracker#1078. The worker was attributed as `omp`, transitioned through the `omp-ext` busy source, and reached its terminal task result.
- The focused secondmate regression in #2043 passes and verifies exact OMP identity, removal of inherited foreign harness markers, both primary extensions, approval mode, model, and `--thinking` propagation. This is deterministic launch coverage, not a real persistent-secondmate run.
- #1376 already contains an opt-in real persistent-secondmate test (`tests/fm-omp-secondmate-live-e2e.test.sh`) covering launch, idle health, marked replies, exit, same-session resume, context, and duplicate refusal. Its useful live scenario should be ported or rerun against the consolidated implementation rather than discarded.
- An OMP 17.2.12 lifecycle probe observed `session_start`, `agent_end`, `session_shutdown` on process exit, and same-process `session_switch`. `session_stop` is appropriate for the direct blocking turn-end callback, but watcher retirement must not treat it as process termination.

One concrete gap in the current #1759 file set is lifecycle control. Current `bin/fm-control-lib.sh` does not admit or map `omp`, and #1759 does not modify `bin/fm-control-lib.sh`, `bin/fm-control.sh`, or `tests/fm-control.test.sh`. That means an OMP worker/secondmate can launch but the supported interrupt/exit/relaunch owner still rejects it. #2043 adds the verified OMP mapping (`Escape`, one delivery, `/exit`, secondmate support) and regression coverage; please absorb that behavior or point to an equivalent owner in this branch.

#1759's native OMP background-job supervision, project-extension preflight, runtime bound, and update path are stronger than #2043's corresponding surface, so I do not propose replacing them. The consolidation target is #1759 plus the lifecycle-control behavior above and a real persistent-secondmate verification derived from #1376.

Thanks for documenting this. As a prospective Firstmate + Orca user, I think this is the right umbrella for closing the gap with the tmux reference backend without trying to make Orca imitate tmux.

A maintainer-friendly path could be incremental:

### Phase 1 — capability-gated supervised worker mode

- Probe `orca agent-context --json` for `worker-start/show/read/stop/abandon/release` and `terminal wait`; do not depend on an unversioned CLI string.
- Persist Orca `run_id`, `task_id`, and `dispatch_id` as the durable task identity. Treat `terminal.handle` as a transient routing hint.
- Keep the current raw worktree + terminal adapter as an explicit compatibility fallback, so this does not regress existing users.
- Use `worker-read --source auto` for bounded transcript-first reads.

### Phase 2 — typed state, delivery, and recovery

- Normalize Orca worker states into Firstmate's backend-neutral state contract instead of inferring lifecycle from terminal text when the supervised-worker capability is available.
- Re-resolve transient terminal routing after restart/reconnect; never send, stop, or release when identity is ambiguous.
- Use `worker-abandon` for honest unknown outcomes and `worker-release` for idempotent, ownership-checked cleanup.
- Surface the active mode in diagnostics: `orca-supervised` versus `orca-terminal-fallback`.

### Phase 3 — persistent homes

After phases 1–2 are proven, evaluate Orca-backed secondmates using a persistent home/current-worktree terminal. I would keep this out of the first patch so ordinary ship/scout reliability lands sooner.

### Suggested acceptance criteria

1. Spawn → receive first worker turn → read → steer → complete → release passes end to end.
2. Restart Orca between spawn and steer; Firstmate rebinds the same dispatch without trusting a stale handle.
3. Restart Firstmate with an unconsumed completion; it reconciles exactly once.
4. A send that only writes PTY bytes but does not start an agent turn is reported as unconfirmed/retryable, never as successful work in flight.
5. Dirty or unlanded work still refuses release.
6. All existing tmux behavior and the Orca compatibility fallback remain unchanged.

The upstream dependencies appear to be:

- stable/canonical addressing: https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/9163
- prompt-consumption confirmation / first-turn deadline: https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/9976
- versioned status/orchestration contract: https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/9810

This split seems attractive because most of the value can land in Firstmate now using Orca's documented worker primitives, while the fallback contains upstream drift.

I suggest preserving two implementation horizons here:

### Immediate adapter defense

- Treat the recorded terminal handle as transient.
- On `terminal_handle_stale` or session start, re-resolve within the recorded worktree using supported stable fields.
- Atomically replace metadata only when exactly one candidate is proven.
- Zero or multiple candidates refuse send/control/teardown and preserve state.

### Durable identity migration

- Once #1813 lands, persist Orca run/task/dispatch identity as authority.
- Resolve current terminal routing through that identity.
- Use worker abandon/release semantics instead of destructive actions keyed only by a cached handle.

The restart smoke proposed in #2084 should exercise both modes: rotate the terminal handle after spawn, verify non-destructive read/send recovery, then verify ambiguous duplicates refuse cleanup. This keeps the current adapter safe without blocking on the upstream canonical-identity fix, while giving a clean deletion path once supervised-worker identity is adopted.

Follow-up tracking is now split so #1813 can stay focused on ordinary ship/scout supervised-worker adoption:

- #2083 — persistent Orca-backed secondmate homes, explicitly gated on this migration and restart-safe identity
- #2084 — capability-gated fake/live compatibility and restart smoke suite for both supervised mode and terminal fallback

This keeps the first implementation bounded while giving the two later concerns independent acceptance criteria and backreferences to the Orca upstream blockers.

## Sync + validation update

**Merge scope.** This branch now carries the federated trunk reconciled against upstream `main`, and it is current with upstream at the time of writing (`0` commits behind). Conflicts were resolved by keeping upstream's structure and re-applying the federated delta onto it, so no remote-only commits were dropped.

**Review fixes.** The no-mistakes review raised 13 findings; 11 were fixed on this branch (2 remaining are informational no-ops). The substantive ones:

- The machine-capacity guard matched process trees against only 7 of 12 verified adapters, so a machine full of the other 5 reported a near-zero fleet footprint and never tripped its memory limit.
- An account helper placed an API key on `env`'s argv, readable from `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`; it now exports into the child instead.
- A shared composer pattern regressed from an alternation to a bracket expression, which matches *bytes* under `LC_ALL=C`, so unrelated box-drawing characters read as an empty composer.
- The shared fleet knowledge base no longer holds a git repository at all, and its directory permissions no longer allow one operator to plant hooks that execute as another.
- `fork-sync.yml` was split so freshly fetched upstream code never executes while a write-scoped credential is reachable: a read-only `validate` job merges and runs the validators, and a gated `publish` job only moves refs.
- Instructions referencing a recovery script that exists in no commit on any ref were removed rather than reworded.

**Gates run locally.** `bin/fm-lint.sh` green across the full canonical set; `bin/fm-test-run.sh --check-coverage` green; both portable parallel lanes and all four portable serial shards green; `bin/fm-doc-audience-check.sh` green. One test failed only under heavy parallel load and passed in isolation and on a clean re-run of its shard. The Herdr lane was deliberately not run locally and is left to CI.

**New CI.** `merge-check.yml` adds only an upstream-merge probe, since `ci.yml` already owns lint and the complete behavior-test partition on every pull request. `fork-sync.yml` keeps the fork current with upstream daily, pushing only a validated clean merge and parking a conflicting one on a `sync/upstream` pull request instead.

**no-mistakes attestation: blocked on infrastructure, not on this code.** The pipeline completes intent, rebase and review, then fails in its test step at `mkdir /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/<run-id>: permission denied`. That path is compiled into no-mistakes v1.41.2 and is a fixed shared `/tmp` location; on this machine it is owned by a different operator, so it collides across users. There is no config or environment override for the evidence root in that version, the shared daemon is serving other lanes and must not be restarted, and storing evidence in-repo is disallowed by this repository's `CONTRIBUTING.md`. The durable fix belongs upstream in no-mistakes as a per-user evidence root.

**Related.** See the supersession note in the description regarding #1559 and #1473.

I wrote and ran an exact scratch regression around the real `bin/fm-watch.sh` and `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` processes.
The fixture exposes one unchanged pane, marks its crewmate `working` through the run-step source, lets the watcher absorb the initial stale observation, then backdates the wedge timer and seeds the same-pane escalation counter at 2.
A second real arm attaches before the next poll, so the next cycle emits escalation 3 with the issue's `demand-deep-inspection` suffix.

The essential regression sequence was:

```sh
# Hermetic fake backend exposes one unchanged pane for a healthy worker.
printf 'working: no-mistakes still advancing\n' > "$state/healthy.status"

# Start the real watcher, then attach a second real arm to that cycle.
FM_FAKE_CREW_STATE='state: working · source: run-step · validating (running)' \
  FM_STALE_ESCALATE_SECS=240 "$WATCH" > "$watcher_out" &
FM_ARM_ATTACH_POLL=0.05 "$WATCH_ARM" > "$arm_out" &

# After the initial stale observation is absorbed, reproduce the repeated
# same-pane escalation described in the issue.
printf '2\n' > "$state/.wedge-escalations-test_fm-healthy"
echo $(( $(date +%s) - 500 )) > "$state/.stale-since-test_fm-healthy"
```

Against pre-fix commit `f5ab7081640561af1890f9b21e72a938983061cf` (the parent of the #1545 merge commit), it reproduces the report exactly:

```text
watcher exit: 0
stale: test:fm-healthy (idle 502s, possible wedge, escalation 3, demand-deep-inspection: same pane has wedge-escalated 3 times in a row - do not re-absorb on the run-step/pane state alone)

attached arm exit: 1
watcher: attached pid=<pid> (beacon 0s)
watcher: FAILED - cycle ended without an actionable reason
```

Against current `main` commit `7f051002b65adb196fdf3804a13d965046782d36`, the same fixture passes:

```text
watcher exit: 0
stale: test:fm-healthy (idle 502s, possible wedge, escalation 3, demand-deep-inspection: same pane has wedge-escalated 3 times in a row - do not re-absorb on the run-step/pane state alone)

attached arm exit: 0
watcher: attached pid=<pid> (beacon 1s)
stale: test:fm-healthy (idle 502s, possible wedge, escalation 3, demand-deep-inspection: same pane has wedge-escalated 3 times in a row - do not re-absorb on the run-step/pane state alone)
```

The current run also records `reason=attached-delivered-wake` in `.watch-cycle-exits.log` and an identity-bound matching entry in `.watch-deliveries.log`.
That is the fix introduced by #1545 at merge commit `88b2a9469418f27e078c3e138001c408c2ff1166`: an attached arm resolves an otherwise unobservable watcher close against the watcher's PID-and-identity-bound terminal-delivery record instead of reporting a false failure.

This fixture uses the hermetic backend seam rather than a live Herdr/macOS session, but it exercises the exact post-delivery arm-layer failure in the report: the full enriched `stale:` reason was emitted and durably queued, then the non-owning attached arm performed close accounting.
That close-accounting path is backend-independent, and the before/after result changes only with #1545's delivery-record implementation.

A second, initiative-specific failure mode is now reproduced against the current scaffold and belongs with this issue's branch-plumbing work.

For an initiative slice, the branch is not merely custom-named:

- the secondmate has already created it at the initiative trunk commit
- the worker must push it because the disposable copy is later released
- the worker must not rebase it onto the repository default branch
- the worker must not open a pull request or push the initiative trunk

Hand-editing only the branch command leaves the ordinary `local-only` rules saying both "never push" and "rebase onto the default branch".
Six of eleven workers in one initiative independently reported that generated-plus-overridden brief as contradictory, each costing a supervisor reconciliation turn; resolving it toward "never push" would lose the slice when the disposable copy is released.

We tested the smaller dedicated contract locally as `--slice-branch <existing-remote-branch>`:

1. It is accepted only with `--mode local-only` on a ship brief.
2. It fetches and checks out the existing remote slice branch rather than creating a default `fm/<task-id>` branch.
3. Its generated rule permits pushing only that slice branch and forbids pushing the trunk/default branch.
4. Its completion contract requires the committed slice branch to be pushed, forbids rebasing onto the default branch, and leaves integration, validation, and the final pull request to the secondmate.
5. Ordinary local-only, direct-PR, and no-mistakes generation stays byte-for-byte on its prior path when the option is absent.
6. Default/integration branch names and wrong task kinds or modes are refused.

The executable `tests/fm-brief.test.sh` behavioral suite passes all of those generated-output cases on current upstream plus the local change, and ShellCheck is clean.
These tests invoke the public brief generator; they do not inspect implementation source text.

A generic `--branch` may still be useful for team naming conventions, but it does not by itself encode this initiative-slice lifecycle and can create the same contradictory or unmergeable shape unless the push, base, integration, and cleanup contracts travel with it.

## Measurements

From `~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl` (`shell.turn.inference_done` records) over a ~15.5h window:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Model calls | 1,187 |
| Total input tokens | 290,264,222 |
| Cached input tokens | 287,391,488 (99.0%) |
| Output tokens | 245,875 |
| Mean input tokens per call | 262,000 |
| Shell tool calls | 1,210 |

Turn-starting prompts, classified by origin:

| Origin | Count |
|---|---|
| Background-task-completion wakes | 234 |
| Actual human messages | ~24 |

Nearly every one of those 234 wakes was `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` completing. Median background-arm duration was **40 seconds**, so the loop is: arm completes -> synthetic user message -> full paid turn on ~262k tokens -> re-arm -> completes 40s later.

Cost attribution over the last top-up window (665 calls, 174,154,757 input tokens, 141 minutes): the balance went from 10,299 credits to 0, about 15 credits per model call, or roughly 59 credits per million input tokens. Because the context is ~99% cached, the spend is almost entirely cache-read on a context that never shrank.

This lines up closely with the original report: watcher-originated activity dominating both call count and cached input.

## A Grok-specific amplifier worth noting

The two supervision protocols differ in a way that matters for cost.

`docs/supervision-protocols/claude.md` states the re-arm happens "with no model command and no model tokens" - it is a Stop hook.

`docs/supervision-protocols/grok.md` has no equivalent. The arm is a tracked background command, and the protocol documents that "Grok injects a synthetic user message with `synthetic_reason: task_completed` when the background arm completes," after which step 4 instructs the model to re-arm. So on Grok **every watcher cycle close bills a full model turn carrying the entire session context**, even when the wake turns out to be benign.

On a 262k-token context at a 40-second median cycle, that is a standing charge of roughly $0.15 per cycle for doing nothing. Codex and Pi appear to sit closer to the Grok shape than the Claude one, which may explain why the original report and this one land on such similar percentages from different vendors.

## Support for the proposed direction

The `fm-wake-context.sh --json` packet proposed above would cut the calls-per-wake multiplier, and I would use it immediately.

It is worth pairing with a second lever, though: the packet reduces *how many* calls each wake costs, but not *what each call costs*. With a ~262k-token context, even a perfectly efficient one-call wake handling is expensive, and #1955 / #560 (always-loaded `AGENTS.md` at ~92KB) are the floor under that number. Both levers multiply.

A third, cheapest lever: on harnesses where the re-arm cannot be free, the arm could avoid waking the model at all when the cycle closes with no actionable reason. Today a benign close still costs a full turn.

Happy to supply the raw aggregation script or fuller per-hour breakdowns if useful.

## Update: the archive-ref split was also cut, as always-inert

The parent change originally kept an archive-ref durability push (`backup/<task-id>-<short-sha>`) for use while a pipeline run is active. Review round 7 established that this clause can never do anything, in any delivery mode, and it has now been removed. **This is probably the most useful single fact in this issue for whoever designs push durability properly**, because it identifies where the real gap is and where it is not.

### The finding, verbatim

> bin/fm-brief.sh:398 tells the worker where to push commits "while a run is active", but bin/fm-brief.sh:395 - three lines earlier in the same block - says "Do not hand-edit, commit, or fix findings yourself while a run is active - the pipeline applies every fix." Trace the prescribed sequence: the worker commits, line 398's first branch pushes fm/<id> to the PR remote before the run starts, the run begins, and from that point line 395 forbids new commits. The pipeline's fix-round commits land in the local gate, not the worker's checkout (confirmed: this review worktree's HEAD is 639ae2d while the author's own head is 62542f8), so during an active run the worker's checkout holds exactly the sha it already pushed. The archive ref therefore has nothing to protect that the pre-run push did not, and line 398's stated rationale for it - "which gets the commits off this disk" - is false in that sequence, because the pre-run push in the same sentence already did that. The only reading under which the archive branch does any work is one where the worker HAS committed during an active run, which line 395 forbids and which desyncs the gate the pipeline is applying fixes to. That misreading is not hypothetical: the round-3 instruction cites a worker that invented exactly this shape mid-run (backup/verified-6690b80f), and this scaffold has repeatedly been corrected on the principle that the reader who needs a rule is the one who will not carry a qualifier forward two lines.

### The cross-mode reasoning, which is stronger than the finding states

The clause is conditioned on a run being **active**, and at that moment there is nothing new to push in any mode:

- **no-mistakes** - the brief forbids committing during a run, so the worker holds only the sha it already pushed before the run started.
- **direct-PR** and **local-only** - there is no run at all, so the condition never fires.

An always-inert clause is worse than no clause: it reads as protection, it will be cited as protection, and it delivers none. That is the same defect class as a literal-phrase test guard reporting a safety it does not provide, which this same change hit twice (see the process lessons in the issue body).

### What this tells a future implementer

**The durable gap is a worker dying while it owns the branch - not anything during a run.** Design for the windows where the worker legitimately holds commits the remote lacks:

1. Between committing and starting a run.
2. After a run ends without publishing (`recover_custody`), when custody has returned.

Do not design for the active-run window. There is nothing there to protect, and instructing a push there invites the forbidden mid-run commit that desyncs the gate.

### Also worth knowing

The `backup/verified-6690b80f` precedent that originally motivated the archive ref came from a worker that had committed mid-run - the very thing the brief forbids. A real-world precedent is not evidence a shape is correct if the situation that produced it was itself out of contract.

## Final update: the push guidance was removed entirely, and here is the hardest case

The parent change shipped the turn rule alone (koopverse/firstmate#13). All push-durability guidance was cut. **Ten review findings, all ten in the push guidance, zero in the turn rule.** The block was reduced four separate times and each reduction produced a new finding rather than converging.

The finding below is why it was cut rather than reduced a fifth time, and it is **the case a future implementer should start from**, because it is invisible in ordinary testing.

### The rebase case, stated precisely

> The push rule is an unscoped standing conditional, so the post-run push you ordered cut in rounds 5 and 7 ("Say NOTHING about pushing after a run reaches a terminal state, in any phrasing") survives by implication. Concrete path: worker commits (sha A), pushes fm/<id> pre-run, runs no-mistakes. The pipeline's rebase step rebases onto a moved base and publishes head B to the same PR remote - ~/.claude/skills/no-mistakes/SKILL.md:10 lists rebase as a pipeline step and :241 calls a diverged preserved head "the ordinary result of the pipeline rebasing your commits onto a newer base". The run returns checks-passed. The pipeline does not move the worker's checkout (this run: author head 62542f8 vs gate head feae3d8), so local HEAD is still A. Now BOTH conditions of line 397 hold - no validation run is in progress, and the remote lacks the worker's commits, since A is not reachable from B - so the standing rule directs `git push <remote> fm/<id>`, which is rejected non-fast-forward. Line 398 forbids force-push, every remedy was cut in rounds 5 and 7, and rule 4 forbids ending the turn in prose, so the worker improvises or stalls at the final moment: the exact outcome this change exists to prevent. The trailing clause "while one is, do not push, wait for it to finish" actively primes that post-run attempt. It does not bite when the base has not moved (in this very run 62542f8's parent IS the base 91a4a6a, so no rebase occurred and the condition is false), which is why it has survived nine rounds.

### Why this is the important part

**The defect is invisible in the run that reviews it.** When the base has not moved, no rebase occurs, the condition is simply false, and every check passes. It fires only when the base has moved - which is the ordinary case in a busy repo and never the case in a run reviewing its own branch.

That is why nine consecutive review rounds missed it while finding other defects in the same five sentences. Any future design must be validated against a **moved base**, not against a quiet one.

### What a future change has to solve

1. **The rebase story** - after the pipeline rebases, the worker's local head is not reachable from the published head. Any condition phrased as "the remote lacks your commits" is true here and directs a push that cannot succeed.
2. **The rejection story** - that push is rejected non-fast-forward. The rule must say what happens next, and "never force-push" without an alternative leaves the worker improvising at the worst moment.
3. **The recovery story** - `recover_custody` is the only state where the worker legitimately holds commits the remote lacks. It is owned by the no-mistakes contract; the brief should point at it, not restate it.

### The pattern, which is the durable lesson

**Every reduction held; every addition generated a finding.** Rounds 5, 7 and 8 each found a defect in mechanism that had been added - an elaborated push block, an archive-ref clause, and a `git log` command written into the rule that turned out to be *fatal* on the first push of every task, when the remote branch does not exist yet. Prefer less text over more precision when both would work.

Related: a check that cannot fail is worse than no check. Three assertions in that work silently succeeded when their subject stopped existing. Negative assertions now require a positive anchor - see the parent PR.

## The rebase case is no longer hypothetical - it reproduced during this change's own delivery

The scenario described above (both push conditions true after a rebase, push rejected non-fast-forward, every remedy already cut) occurred for real about forty minutes after it was written, while delivering the parent change. Recording it here because a concrete reproduction is worth more to a future implementer than the analysis alone.

### What happened

The eleven commits on the branch had to be re-authored (they had landed under the wrong author). Re-authoring rewrites every commit, so the new head necessarily diverged from the published one:

```
gate head:   0d01a891   (old authorship)
origin head: 0d01a891   (same, on the open PR)
new head:    f5ba0a95   (re-authored)
0d01a891 is NOT an ancestor of f5ba0a95
```

The push to the pipeline gate was then rejected:

```
git push no-mistakes HEAD:refs/heads/fm/<task>
 ! [rejected]  (non-fast-forward)
```

This is the predicted shape exactly: the worker holds commits the remote lacks, no validation run is in progress, so a standing "push whenever the remote lacks your commits" rule fires - and the push cannot succeed. Had the cut push guidance still shipped, a worker here would have been instructed into this push, forbidden from force-pushing, forbidden from ending the turn in prose, and left with no instructed next step.

### What resolved it, and why it is not a rule you can write into a scaffold

The resolution needed a human decision and three preconditions that no standing instruction can assert on a worker's behalf:

1. **An explicit, scoped authorisation** - force-push this one branch, for this one rewrite, with `--force-with-lease` and never plain `--force`.
2. **Proof that nothing would be lost** - the old and new trees were compared and found identical (`ec1129cf...` both sides), plus a filtered three-dot patch comparison with index lines stripped, since raw patches differ on index lines alone and would produce a false alarm.
3. **The lease itself** as the safety mechanism - if anyone else had moved the branch, the push fails rather than overwriting them. The instruction explicitly forbade escalating to plain `--force` if the lease rejected.

That is the real shape of the recovery story: a scoped human authorisation, an equivalence proof, and a lease. A scaffold sentence cannot supply any of the three, which is the strongest argument yet that this belongs in tooling with a real decision point rather than in prose telling a worker to push.

### Additional lesson from the same delivery: a complete-looking check census

Also worth recording, because it is the same family as the check-that-cannot-fail problem. The parent PR was reported green off 14 check-runs, all `completed`/`success`, with no `in_progress` or `queued` - a correct per-job read. It was still wrong: a **15th** check-run landed four minutes later and **failed**. The set was incomplete at the moment of the census, and an incomplete set looks exactly like a complete one.

**The durable check is `mergeable_state` plus the required-check list - never a count of whatever has finished.** A census taken early is indistinguishable from a census taken late until the late job arrives.

We hit this same symptom (watcher wedges silently within minutes of arming, beacon frozen, watch lock held by the wedged pid, every re-arm wedges again) on `b5d430d`-era code and root-caused it while working on an unrelated change. Sharing in case it saves someone the dig:

**Root cause we proved locally:** the fleet locks are non-reentrant, and `bin/fm-watch.sh` traps `HUP/INT/TERM` as `exit 1`, which unwinds into `watcher_cleanup` - and `watcher_cleanup` re-acquires locks the interrupted flow still holds, so the process spins forever in `fm_lock_acquire_wait` on a lock its own pid owns. The window is reachable on **every poll** via `_fm_recovery_marker_arm_check`, not only via `fm_wake_append`, which is why it reproduces so readily.

Concrete observation backing this: a wedged watcher whose own pid held both `.wake-queue.lock` and `.watcher-down.lock` with a beacon frozen for 64 minutes.

Two fix shapes we scoped (both have sharp edges):
1. A global deferred-signal trap in `fm-watch.sh` with explicit safe points each poll - correct shape, but any code path that misses a safe point risks a TERM-immune watcher.
2. Making `fm_lock_acquire_wait` ownership-aware - small change, but roughly a third of its ~65 callers ignore its return value, so naive ownership-awareness silently unlocks critical sections across spawn/teardown/drain; every caller needs auditing.

The afk daemon's SIGTERM shutdown hang (#2270) looks like the same unwind-into-cleanup pattern on the daemon path and may share the fix.

We independently hit this exact defect on our fork before finding this PR, and can confirm the fix direction.

We saw it on non-prime-agent panes running the `pi` harness: six agent sessions had genuinely exited, but each pane's Herdr registration was left behind reporting `agent_status=done`/`idle`. The panes stayed alive from Herdr's point of view, and our own liveness checks kept reporting the agent as `alive` for hours — no automatic relaunch could happen because the guard read a present agent. Root cause on our side was the same one this PR documents: a cleanly exited agent never calls a release/deregister step, so the status word alone is not a liveness signal and a `done`/`idle` record can just as easily mean "finished a turn, still resident" as "process is gone."

Our own fix (independent, smaller in scope, no subtree walk) took the same approach this PR takes: before trusting a registered status as `live`, read the pane's actual foreground process. Only-shell-left demotes to dead; any non-shell process (including a genuinely waiting `pi`) stays live; any unreadable/unparseable read stays conservatively live rather than declaring the agent dead. That matches the corroboration principle this PR states plainly: "No herdr `agent_status` means 'exited'."

One thing worth flagging for review here: PR #2070 fixes the same underlying husk-classification problem, but only for `agent == prime-agent` (via its foreground + subtree probes). This PR generalizes the corroboration to every agent kind via `pane process-info`, which is what actually closes the gap we hit — #2070 alone would not have covered our case since we don't run prime-agent. Worth confirming the two don't end up duplicating logic if both land.

My proposal, two edits to bin/fm-brief.sh, applied to both the ship and scout scaffolds.

1. Rule 2 gains a pointer, so the file rule stops reading as complete:

▎ Stay inside this worktree; modify nothing outside it. That is a rule about files; shared administration is rule 7 and is not covered by staying inside your own directory.

2. Rule 7 absorbs the pool rather than gaining a neighbour:

▎ Shared infrastructure is firstmate's, never yours. Rule 2 governs this worktree's contents; the worktree itself, the pool it was leased from, the repository every lane's worktree shares, and the no-mistakes daemon are each ONE instance serving every lane and home, so an action that looks local here hits every other lane at once - and those lanes are running right now.
▎ Never create, remove, return, prune, move, or reassign any worktree or pool slot in that shared pool or its shared repository, and never do any of that to a worktree you did not create: git worktree add/remove/prune, treehouse get/return, orca worktree create/rm, and the equivalent on whatever other worktree provider is in use are all forbidden there, including on worktrees that look stale or unused, and including this one - firstmate discards yours at teardown.
▎ Never delete or rewrite a branch or ref that is not yours - another task's branch, or a shared branch such as the default one. Never stop, restart, or update the no-mistakes daemon.
▎ Removing a worktree from inside a lane destroys the working copy of whatever lane owns it, mid-run, so there is no safe local workaround - when you need a second checkout, a worktree or branch action, a daemon action, or anything else on that list, and on ANY no-mistakes daemon error, stop and report it through rule 4's status protocol: what you need and why, quoting any error text verbatim. Firstmate does it for you.

Four things that wording is deliberately doing, each of which I got wrong first:

- Names the act, not the provider. Naming one provider leaves the hole open on every other backend.
- Scopes to the shared pool and to worktrees you did not create. A categorical ban collides with the validation pipeline, which creates and prunes its own gate worktree - so a literal reading forbids the very thing the same brief mandates.
- Says whose branch, and nothing about pushing. "A branch you did not create" catches a relaunched worker inheriting its own task branch, whose instructions then tell it to rebase.
- Points at rule 4 rather than restating it. The exit must be real or the rule gets broken, but re-specifying the status verb duplicates a contract rule 4 already owns.

Testing: assert it by generating a brief and reading the output, for both scaffolds and every delivery mode - not by grepping the script, which only proves the string exists rather than that a worker receives it.

Concrete reproduction of the post-landing convergence gap described here:

- Firstmate home used the Herdr backend for a FloCafe ship task.
- The task's PR (#276) merged successfully with green checks.
- The worker process/pane then disappeared, but the task record and recorded Herdr endpoint remained present.
- The shared session kept an agentless pane slot, and the watcher continued hashing/classifying it instead of retiring the endpoint or creating one durable cleanup obligation.
- The unchanged slot generated repeated `stale:` wedge notifications roughly every four minutes, reaching 117 consecutive escalations and repeated `demand-deep-inspection` prompts.
- The remote delivery branch also remained until manual deletion.

Cleanup could not safely delete the isolated copy automatically because it contained two local commits not included in the merged PR, so preserving that copy was correct. The defect is that the completed task's endpoint and watcher bookkeeping were not retired or quarantined separately from the preserved local work.

This appears to be a Firstmate lifecycle/reconciliation issue, not a no-mistakes validation failure and not primarily a Herdr server failure. Herdr exposed the dead pane; Firstmate continued treating the recorded endpoint as a watchable window after the task reached a terminal delivery outcome. A fix should preserve dirty/unlanded work while retiring or suppressing the dead endpoint and making any branch/copy cleanup refusal durable and actionable, rather than repeatedly escalating the same orphaned pane.

Follow-up classification: this is not primarily a Herdr defect or a no-mistakes defect.

Herdr exposed the condition by retaining an agentless pane slot after the worker exited, but Firstmate owns the durable task metadata, terminal-outcome reconciliation, watcher candidate inventory, and cleanup/refusal lifecycle. The repeated alerts continued because Firstmate still treated the recorded `window=main:wT:p2` as an active watch candidate after PR #276 was merged and the endpoint reported dead.

This is related to the post-landing convergence problem in this RFC, with a narrower immediate symptom: terminal task endpoint retirement/suppression and durable cleanup obligations are missing or incomplete. It overlaps most closely with #1337 (Herdr presentation journal retirement) and #882 (terminal pane alert flooding), but is distinct because the pane is dead/agentless and the task record itself remains in-flight while the local copy must be preserved for unlanded commits.

I did not create a duplicate issue. Please consider this concrete reproduction when implementing the lifecycle reconciliation and terminal endpoint retirement path.

Correcting my own hypothesis in the report above, with a verified mechanism.

I originally guessed that selection preferred a terminal run over a concurrently-matching live one. That guess was wrong, and so was an earlier one I made about head staleness. Here is what I actually verified.

**The live run's head is not present in the worktree's object store**, so the documented match condition can never be satisfied — no ancestry relation can be computed at all.

Sampling the worktree HEAD and the run head **in the same command** (my earlier comparisons mixed values captured minutes apart, which is how I misread this twice):

```
worktree HEAD: da8d9b9bc76fd6e93365dab6c98b3bd92b23774a
run head     : ef4781f2
reader       : state: failed · source: run-step · run failed
axi status   : status: running

$ git -C <worktree> merge-base --is-ancestor da8d9b9b ef4781f2 ; echo $?
1
$ git -C <worktree> cat-file -t ef4781f2
fatal: Not a valid object name ef4781f2
$ git -C <worktree> merge-base da8d9b9b ef4781f2
<exit 128, no merge base>
```

The header documents the intended rule as: run head equals worktree HEAD, or worktree HEAD is an ancestor of the run head (pipeline fix commits advanced the run on the same line), while local work that advanced past the run head must not be attributed.

With the run head object absent locally, **none of those three relations is computable**. The pipeline is committing its fix rounds in its own custody, and those objects are not in the worker's repository at the moment the reader runs.

**The part I would call the defect:** that unresolvable state is reported as `failed` rather than as unknown or unattributable. Refusing to attribute the run looks correct and deliberate; presenting the refusal as a terminal failure verdict is what makes fleet status wrong. A supervisor cannot distinguish "this lane's run failed" from "I could not correlate this lane's run", and those warrant opposite responses.

This still reproduces continuously — the three lanes in the report remain `running` in their worktrees and `failed` to the reader.

Confidence: the observations and commands above are verified and repeatable. Which code path produces the `failed` fallback once correlation fails, I have not traced.

Confirming this, with a standalone reproduction and two further failure modes.

**Version:** `bb15d151c47b88de0ee9441a5f24904f43f76fa1`, `bin/fm-classify-lib.sh` last touched in `d8bb074`. macOS, bash 3.2.

**Minimal reproduction:**

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -eu
REPO=${1:?usage: run.sh /path/to/firstmate}
d=$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p "$d/state"
printf 'needs-decision [key=alpha]: token BEFORE the colon\n'  > "$d/state/good.status"
printf 'needs-decision: [key=alpha] token AFTER the colon\n'   > "$d/state/bad.status"
. "$REPO/bin/fm-classify-lib.sh"
echo "good.status folds to: $(status_open_decisions "$d/state/good.status" | cut -f1)"
echo "bad.status  folds to: $(status_open_decisions "$d/state/bad.status"  | cut -f1)"
```

```
good.status folds to: alpha
bad.status  folds to: default
```

I bisected the trigger: colon placement is the only variable. Key length, hyphens, quotes or brackets in the note, note length (tested to 2,077 bytes), the cursor in `state/.<id>.open-decisions-cursor`, and `_fm_decision_drop`'s matching are all irrelevant. The whole-file and cursor-backed folds agree byte for byte, including after a forced re-fold.

**Three things I think are worth adding.**

**1. The `OPEN DECISIONS` listing makes a defaulted decision look keyed.** This is why the bug is hard to spot rather than merely annoying. `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh:96-100` omits `[key=...]` when the key is `default`, but the discarded token is still sitting in the note it prints verbatim:

```
OPEN DECISIONS (still open, folded from the durable status logs - not just the latest line):
tk  needs-decision: [key=alpha] token AFTER the colon
tk2 [key=alpha] needs-decision: token BEFORE the colon
OPEN DECISIONS: close one by answering it: bin/fm-send.sh <task> --resolve-key <key> '<answer>'
```

Only `tk2` has a key. The rows differ only in where `[key=...]` sits, in long wrapped lines, directly above a hint telling the reader to pass `--resolve-key <key>`. Fixing `_fm_decision_key` alone would leave every already-written malformed line still rendering this way, so I would refuse to fold a line carrying an unparsed `[key=` token, or render defaulted rows distinguishably.

**2. A malformed `resolved:` closes an unrelated decision.** The issue covers overwrite; this is the other direction:

```
needs-decision: [key=alpha] first decision, still unanswered
resolved: [key=beta] closing a completely different decision
-> status_open_decisions prints nothing
```

Both fold to `default`, so `beta`'s resolution clears `alpha`. This is reachable directly from the scaffold guidance that tells a worker to self-close with `resolved: {how it cleared}` "(same `[key=<slug>]` if you opened it with one)".

**3. It bypasses the reserved-key namespace protection.** A `pending-reply-*` escalation in the malformed form folds to `default`, so `_fm_decision_key_transition_allowed` never applies:

```
blocked: [key=pending-reply-abcdef0123456789] pending-reply-missed: ...
resolved [key=pending-reply-abcdef0123456789]: pending-reply-resolved: ...
-> default  blocked  [key=pending-reply-abcdef0123456789] pending-reply-missed: ...
```

The owner's correct resolution cannot close it, and any unrelated bare `resolved:` can. That is the takeover the reserved-namespace rule exists to prevent.

**On the suggested fixes:** I would do both rather than either. If `_fm_decision_key` is widened to scan the whole line, `FM_OPEN_DECISIONS_FOLD_VERSION` (`bin/fm-classify-lib.sh:387`) needs bumping in the same change, since its own contract requires that when fold semantics change and existing cursors would otherwise keep serving the old `default`-bucketed set.

On the scaffold half, the malformed form appears to be what the guidance describes rather than a mistake. `bin/fm-brief.sh:325-334` and `:446-450` give a worker `needs-decision: {summary of options}` and, separately, `resolved: {how it cleared}` "(same `[key=<slug>]` if you opened it with one)". Composing those two produces the broken form. The only correctly-formed keyed example in that file is at `:246-247` (`working [key=<work-slug>]:`), in a separate scaffold those workers never receive.

**Test coverage:** every fixture in `tests/fm-wake-drain-open-decisions.test.sh` and `tests/fm-send-resolve-key.test.sh` uses the working `verb [key=X]:` form. Nothing exercises `verb: [key=X]`, which is why this got through.

Happy to send a PR for either half if that is useful.

## Verified consequence for claude dispatch profiles

`--permission-mode auto` exists only for the models Claude Code supports it on. Any other model starts **silently in Manual mode** and parks an unattended crewmate on its first permission prompt.

Verified 2026-08-18 on Claude Code 2.1.234 as root (footers captured in `docs/verification/claude.md`):

```text
--model claude-fable-5             ⏵⏵ auto mode on (shift+tab to cycle)
--model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001  ⏸ manual mode on · auto mode unavailable for this model
```

Consequence: a claude dispatch profile (`config/crew-dispatch.json`) or `config/secondmate-harness` model token **must name an auto-capable model: Opus 4.6+, Sonnet 4.6+, or Fable 5** (the list Claude Code documents today; the harness-adapters skill and `claude auto-mode defaults` own the current one). Older models such as Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and Opus 4.5 are not launchable unattended on this template. The post-spawn peek should show `auto mode on`; a `manual mode on` footer is a launch failure to relaunch on a supported model, not a prompt to answer by hand.

The tracked example `docs/examples/crew-dispatch.json` was moved off `haiku` to `claude-sonnet-5` in this PR for that reason.

Follow-up evidence on `tests/fm-wake-queue.test.sh`, which I could not get to completion on Windows in the original writeup. It resolved, and the result strengthens the case for this change.

**The suite hangs on unmodified `HEAD`, at the bug this PR fixes.** Traced against a clean `HEAD` worktree, it stalls in the `self-held-lock` fixture at:

```
fm_lock_acquire_wait "$lock" || exit 10
```

sourcing `HEAD`'s own `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh`. That is cause 3 from the description: `ln -s` copies instead of linking, `fm_lock_points_to_owner` can never confirm ownership, and the wait spins forever.

**Reduced to the smallest case** — one `fm_wake_append` against a scratch state dir:

| Single wake append, Windows 11 / Git Bash | Result |
|---|---|
| unmodified `HEAD` | never completes (killed at 6m40s) |
| this branch | completes, 16.3s |

So on Windows today the durable wake queue cannot be written at all. It is not only the session lock that is broken — supervision cannot function either, because every append hangs.

**On this branch the suite gets further and passes what `HEAD` hangs on:**

```
ok - an abandoned same-process lock hold is reclaimed; a parent's live hold is not
ok - self-announced appends suppress only their own bytes and fail toward waking
ok - historical annotations replay nothing already announced and keep everything new
```

3 passed, 0 failed. The first of those is the very fixture that hangs on `HEAD`.

**Remaining honest caveat.** The suite still does not run to completion here. It stops progressing in the concurrency stress case that forks 41 simultaneous `fm_wake_append` writers and waits on all of them. Measured directly, that is slowness rather than deadlock — every record does land in the queue:

| Concurrent writers | Elapsed | Records queued |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 26s | 1 |
| 2 | 44s | 2 |
| 4 | 200s | 4 |
| 8 | 254s | 7 of 8 within the window |

At roughly 16-26s per append on MSYS, 41 concurrent writers need far longer than any timeout I ran. I have not reduced that cost, and I am not claiming this suite green on Windows. Adjacent Windows finding from the same session, same root cause family (symlinks), but a separate defect from the one this PR fixes. Reporting it here rather than opening an issue since it is the same platform story; happy to split it out if you would prefer.

**Every skill is silently unavailable on a Windows checkout.**

`.claude/skills` is tracked as a symlink to `../.agents/skills`:

```
$ git ls-files -s .claude/skills
120000 2b7a412b8fa0fb7e985b0793321bd4e698f2b6cd 0	.claude/skills
```

Git for Windows defaults to `core.symlinks=false`. The entry then materialises as an ordinary 17-byte text file whose contents are the link target:

```
$ ls -la .claude/
-rw-r--r-- 1 user 197121   17 .claude/skills
$ cat .claude/skills
../.agents/skills
```

The harness finds no `.claude/skills` directory, so none of the 19 skills under `.agents/skills/` are discoverable — `stow`, `afk`, `bearings`, `harness-adapters`, `project-management`, `secondmate-provisioning`, and the rest. `AGENTS.md` instructs the agent to load several of them at precise triggers, and every one of those loads fails.

**What makes this worse than the lock bug: it fails invisibly.** The lock bug announces itself on every session start with a read-only banner. This one produces no warning at all. An agent following `AGENTS.md` simply cannot load the skill it is told to load, and nothing anywhere says why. I only found it because a captain asked for `/stow` by name — otherwise the degradation is silent and total.

**Repair on an affected clone:**

```bash
git config core.symlinks true
rm -f .claude/skills
MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict ln -s ../.agents/skills .claude/skills
```

`git status` is clean afterwards, confirming the symlink is what the index always intended. The skills were picked up mid-session with no restart. It is the only tracked symlink in the repo, so nothing else is affected:

```bash
git ls-files -s | awk '$1=="120000"{print $4}'   # .claude/skills, and nothing else
```

Native symlink creation needs Windows Developer Mode or an elevated shell — the same prerequisite this PR's `MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict` change relies on.

**Possible upstream fixes**, in rough order of how much they ask of the user — I have not implemented any of these, so treat them as suggestions rather than a proposal:

1. A `SETUP`/README note for Windows telling users to set `core.symlinks=true` before cloning. Cheapest, but it only helps people who read it before the fact.
2. A bootstrap check that verifies `.claude/skills` resolves and prints an actionable diagnostic when it does not. This fits the existing detect-then-consent bootstrap pattern and would have surfaced the problem immediately, which is the part that actually failed here.
3. Ship the directory rather than the symlink — for example `.claude/skills` as a real directory, or generating the link at bootstrap. Larger change, and I have not thought through the consequences for non-Windows installs.

Option 2 seems the best fit to me, since the real failure was the silence rather than the broken link. But you know the repo's constraints better than I do.
